title: Server Log
explain: A server log keeps many clients in sync without refetching everything. The server appends every change to a numbered log and also keeps the current state; each client remembers the last log id it applied and asks for everything after it. If a client has been away so long that the log was compacted past its cursor, it reconciles against the current state instead.
model:
The server keeps two things:

- A **change log**: `incremental_id -> entity_id -> revision` (IDs only increase; the entry may point at the entity rather than carry its payload).
- The **current state** of every entity.

```
log:    901 e7 r4 | 902 e2 r9 | 903 e7 r5 | 904 e5 r1 | ...   latest = 1260
client: cursor = 1200  --ask for 1201..1260-->  fetch the entities they name --> apply --> cursor = 1260
```

- **Resume:** the client sends its `current_cursor`; the server returns `cursor + 1 ... latest`.
- **Apply idempotently:** skip an entry whose revision is not newer than the local copy.
- **Bootstrap:** a new client takes the current state (not the log) and the log position that state corresponds to, from one consistent snapshot, then follows the log from there.
- **Compaction:** the server periodically snapshots and compacts the log. A client whose cursor is older than the oldest retained entry has nothing to replay and must **reconcile with the current state**, then take a fresh cursor.

details.q: How many entries does a client with cursor 1,200 fetch when the latest log id is 1,260?
details.a: Entries 1,201 through 1,260: 60 of them (1,260 - 1,200). It then sets its cursor to 1,260. Store the cursor last, after applying the changes.

details.q: Why must applying a log entry be idempotent and revision-guarded?
details.a: A crash between applying and storing the cursor replays a range, and a client may also fetch an entity directly. Example: a client already holds entity 7 at revision 6 and the replay delivers (id 905, entity 7, revision 5); it ignores it because it is not newer. That makes overlapping ranges and mixed log and direct fetches safe.

details.q: A phone was offline for a month. Its cursor is 1,200 and the oldest retained entry is now 1,500. What happens?
details.a: Entries 1,201 to 1,499 no longer exist, so replaying from 1,500 would silently skip changes. The server answers 'cursor too old' and the client reconciles with the current state (full resync, or a diff by revision), then takes a new cursor.

details.q: A new client reads all entities and only afterwards asks for the latest log id to use as its cursor. What can go wrong?
details.a: Changes committed between the two reads are included in the cursor but not in the client's copy, so they are never replayed and the copy is silently wrong. Read the state together with the log position it corresponds to, in one consistent snapshot, and start catching up right after that position.

details.q: Plain truncation or compaction: how do they differ for clients?
details.a: Truncating drops old entries, so every client behind the cut must fully resync. Compaction that keeps the newest entry per entity (plus tombstones for deletes, kept long enough) lets many lagging clients still catch up, because intermediate revisions are redundant.

details.q: How long should you retain the log?
details.a: Longer retention means fewer full resyncs but more storage. Size it for realistic offline periods (a phone in a drawer for a week), and make the full-resync path cheap and rate-limited, because a bad release can send everyone there at once.

details.q: How does this relate to a cursor and to a change feed?
details.a: The client's position is a [cursor](#/sd/f/cursor); the server side is the same idea as a [change feed](#/sd/f/change-feed) with explicit revisions so that clients can be idempotent. [ETag](#/sd/f/etag) revisions give the cheap 'has this one entity changed?' check.

prompts.q: Explain a server log sync protocol: what the server stores and what the client stores.
points: Server: append-only log of id, entity, revision, plus current state
Resume by asking for cursor + 1 to latest, fetch entities, apply
Revision-guarded, idempotent apply; store the cursor last

prompts.q: Walk through bootstrapping a new client without losing changes.
points: Take current state and the log position it corresponds to together
One consistent snapshot, not two separate reads
Follow the log from that position
Reading the position afterwards can miss changes

prompts.q: The log is compacted and a client returns after a month. What happens?
points: Cursor older than the oldest retained entry
Client reconciles with current state (full resync or revision diff)
Retention is a storage vs resync trade-off
